title: Milk Street to Tower Hill: the Under-Sheriff, the Island of Nowhere, and the Oath Not Sworn
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Milk Street, City of London: the birth
stops.date_confidence: Day and year attested (7 February 1478, thomasmorestudies.org chronology; Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'). The street is not. Only London is secure; Milk Street is family and local tradition, and Joanne Paul's archival work treats the exact birth house as disputed. Pinned at Milk Street because that is where the tradition puts it, tagged [R] for the address.
stops.campa: On the seventh of February a son is born in the City of London to John More, lawyer of Lincoln's Inn, and his wife Agnes Graunger, daughter of a City alderman. The family and the neighbourhood will remember the house as one in Milk Street, off Cheapside, in the ward of the mercers and the goldsmiths; the parish paper that would settle it does not survive, and the address is tradition rather than record. The Guildhall, where he will sit as under-sheriff for eight years, stands a quarter of a mile off. The child is christened Thomas.
suggested_refs: The Milk Street site in the ward of Cripplegate, traditional birthplace of Thomas More
sources: Joanne Paul, archival work on the More birthplace (cited in the dossier, not reached directly)

stops.name: St Anthony's School, Threadneedle Street: the Latin grammar
stops.date_confidence: Range, not a point. thomasmorestudies.org/chronology/ gives 'c. 1484-1489 Attends St. Anthony's School, London (7-12)'. Wikipedia and Luminarium compress this to a single year, 1485; that compression is an artefact of the chronologies, not evidence. Dated here to the opening of the range and defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He is sent up Threadneedle Street to St Anthony's, the strongest of the City grammar schools, where boys of seven and twelve construe Latin aloud and dispute against the boys of St Paul's in the churchyard. Five or six years of accidence and syntax give him the language he will think in for the rest of his life. The Utopia, the Responsio, the History of King Richard III and the letters out of prison are all written in it, and the English works read in places like a man translating himself back. Nothing else about these years is on record.
suggested_refs: St Anthony's Hospital School, Threadneedle Street, dissolved under Edward VI

stops.name: Lambeth Palace: the page at Morton's table
stops.date_confidence: Sources disagree on the years and none can be preferred. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More' gives 1490-1492; thomasmorestudies.org/chronology/ gives 'c. 1489-1491 Page for Archbishop and Chancellor Morton (12-14)'. Rendered here as c.1489/1490-1492, dated to the earliest reading. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's Lambeth Palace figures (51.49556N, 0.11972W); the dossier's -0.1219 sat in the river. Morton's prediction is Roper writing sixty years later and is a biographical motif, not a transcript.
stops.campa: At about twelve he is placed in the household of John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor of England, and waits at the archbishop's table in the hall at Lambeth, across the river from Westminster. He learns there how the crown and the church do business with one another, and how a man standing between them serves both at once. Morton, an old politician who had outlived Richard III, watches the boy step into the Christmas interludes unrehearsed and make a part of his own, and says something to his guests that the boy's son-in-law will still be repeating in the 1550s.
stops.quote: This child here waiting at the table, whosoever shall live to see it, will prove a marvelous man.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.2
suggested_refs: Lambeth Palace, the archbishop's London residence and Morton's household
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Oxford: two years of the new learning
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Thomas More' and Luminarium give entry in 1492; Roper-derived chronologies give c.1491-1493. Which hall, Canterbury College or St Mary Hall, is disputed and not resolvable from any source reached. Pinned at the Canterbury College site.
stops.campa: Morton sends him on to Oxford, where he spends about two years in Greek and Latin among the men bringing the new learning back from Italy, Thomas Linacre and William Grocyn among them. His father keeps him short of money on principle, so that the son shall learn nothing of dice and everything of grammar. Then John More, judging that Greek will not feed a household, calls him home to the law. He is about fifteen, and he keeps the Greek. Which hall held him, Canterbury College or St Mary Hall, the record does not fix, and no source reached settles it.
suggested_refs: The site of Canterbury College, absorbed into Christ Church, Oxford
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: New Inn, Wych Street: the father's redirection
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Thomas More' gives 1494 for the move to New Inn; Roper-derived chronology gives c.1493-1495. Attested that the Inn of Chancery preceded Lincoln's Inn; the exact year is soft. Wych Street itself was demolished for the Aldwych in 1901 and the pin is the historic line of the street.
stops.campa: He enters New Inn on Wych Street, one of the Inns of Chancery where boys learn the writs and the forms before they are thought fit for an Inn of Court. What he takes up here is the common law of England: unwritten, precedent laid on precedent, learned by watching and by arguing in hall rather than out of any book. It is his father's trade and his grandfather's city. For the rest of his life he will hold that a law of England is a thing made by men in Parliament and binding on the king's subjects because it was made. He is about sixteen when he starts.
suggested_refs: Wych Street and the Inns of Chancery, cleared for the Aldwych in 1901
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Lincoln's Inn: called to the bar
stops.date_confidence: Admission to Lincoln's Inn 1496 attested (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; Luminarium). The call to the bar is given as 1501 by Luminarium and 1502 by Wikipedia; the two traditions are recorded, not reconciled. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's Lincoln's Inn figures (51.5171250N, 0.1145778W). The dossier's added 'reader 1511, treasurer 1512' is dropped here: it is sourced to nothing reachable, the Lincoln's Inn article does not mention More at all, and thomasmorestudies.org carries no such entries.
stops.campa: Admitted to Lincoln's Inn in Chancery Lane, his father's own house, he reads there for the bar and is called to it in 1501 or 1502, depending which chronology is opened. He is now a common lawyer of the City, with his father's connections behind him and his own tongue in front. He argues, he pleads, he lectures. He also keeps, through the same years, a discipline of prayer and fasting that his fellow students find excessive in a young man with a career to make, and does not explain it to them.
suggested_refs: Lincoln's Inn, Chancery Lane, admission 1496

stops.name: St Lawrence Jewry, Guildhall Yard: the layman on the City of God
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 1501 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy chronology, 'Thomas More'; Roper). Month unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Roper adds Grocyn among the hearers.
stops.campa: At the church beside Guildhall Yard a layman not yet twenty-five stands up and lectures publicly on Augustine's City of God, and the scholars of London come in to hear him, Grocyn among them. He does not preach. He expounds, the way a reader in an Inn expounds a statute, taking the twenty-two books of the African bishop as a text to be construed clause by clause. Augustine's argument is that the earthly city and the city of God are two commonwealths grown into each other and told apart only at the end of the world. No text of the lectures survives.
suggested_refs: St Lawrence Jewry, Guildhall Yard, rebuilt by Wren after 1666
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas More' chronology
William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: London Charterhouse, Charterhouse Square: four years beside the Carthusians
stops.date_confidence: Range, and the dossier carried it twice. thomasmorestudies.org/chronology/ gives 'c. 1501-1504 Frequents Charterhouse (Carthusians)'; Wikipedia gives 1503-1504. The dossier separately logged the same episode at 1504 with an [R] tag, and that second entry misplaced the City of God lectures at the Charterhouse; they belong at St Lawrence Jewry. Merged here at c.1501-1504. The hair shirt and the severity of practice are Erasmus (to Ulrich von Hutten, 23 July 1519) and Roper, both friends writing for the record, and are [R].
stops.campa: For something like four years he lodges beside the Carthusians at Charterhouse Square, keeps their hours, and tests whether he belongs inside the wall. Erasmus, writing to Ulrich von Hutten in 1519, says he wore a hair shirt against the skin and used a scourge; Roper says the same, and both are friends of the house writing to be believed. What is not in doubt is that he never took the habit. He goes out instead into the arrangement he will hold for thirty years, a lay life run on a monk's timetable: a wife, children, a City practice, and the hair shirt underneath the chain of office.
suggested_refs: Erasmus to Ulrich von Hutten, 23 July 1519, the fullest contemporary description of More's person and habits
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Palace of Westminster: the subsidy cut down
stops.date_confidence: The Parliament seat for Great Yarmouth in 1504 is documented (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'). The leadership of the opposition to Henry VII's subsidy, and the reprisal against John More, are Roper's family tradition and are doubted by modern scholars; tagged [R] and left standing as tradition, not resolved.
stops.campa: Sitting for Great Yarmouth in the Parliament of 1504, he speaks against the subsidy Henry VII has demanded for his daughter's marriage, and the Commons cut the grant well below what was asked. He keeps out of the king's sight for the remaining five years of the reign. Roper's account, written half a century later inside the family, adds that the king could not reach the son and so had the father arrested and fined a hundred pounds in the Tower. Historians since have doubted it. No writ has been produced, and the seat is the only part of the episode that is documented.
suggested_refs: The Parliament of 1504 and the subsidy for the marriage of Margaret Tudor
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Netherhall, Roydon, Essex: the marriage to Jane Colt
stops.date_confidence: Marriage in 1505 to Jane (Joanna) Colt of Netherhall attested (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; Roper). Month unknown, defaulted. COORDINATE CORRECTED: the dossier's 51.7719/0.1725 fell about nine kilometres east of Roydon, in open country toward Sheering. Roydon village is 51.773N, 0.0396E per Wikipedia; the Nether Hall moated site lies north-east of it and is pinned here at 51.7740, 0.0450. The preferred-sister anecdote is Roper family tradition, [R], and cannot be checked.
stops.campa: He rides out into Essex to the moated house of John Colt at Roydon and marries the eldest daughter, Jane, who is about seventeen and has been raised in the country with no Latin and little music. Roper's family story, which he had from inside the household, is that More preferred the second sister and married the first so as not to shame her by passing her over. It cannot be checked and never has been. What is on record is four children in six years, Margaret, Elizabeth, Cecily and John, and a husband teaching his wife to read Latin and to play.
suggested_refs: The Nether Hall moated site at Roydon, Essex, seat of the Colt family
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Bucklersbury, City of London: the house of Latin daughters
stops.date_confidence: Residence at Bucklersbury from 1505 attested (Roper; Wikipedia). The Lucian translations with Erasmus, 1506, are given by the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology and Luminarium and described in the humanist correspondence as a friendly contest, tagged [R] for the contest framing. Jane Colt's death and the remarriage to Alice Middleton within weeks are attested for 1511 and are carried into this stop rather than given a pin of their own.
stops.campa: The married household sets up in Bucklersbury, a street of grocers and apothecaries running off the Poultry, and here the daughters are put to Greek, Latin, logic and astronomy on exactly the terms a son would have had. Erasmus lodges with them, and the two friends race each other turning Lucian's dialogues out of Greek into Latin, printing the results together in 1506. In 1511 Jane dies, twenty-three or so. Within weeks More marries Alice Middleton, a widow some years older, unlettered, blunt in speech, and a competent manager of a house that is about to get much larger.
suggested_refs: Luciani opuscula, the More and Erasmus Lucian translations, Paris 1506
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas More' chronology

stops.name: Bucklersbury, City of London: the Life of John Pico
stops.date_confidence: Publication of The Life of John Pico, Earl of Mirandola dated 1510 by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy chronology. Month unknown, defaulted. Pinned at the household rather than a printing house; the printer is not established by any source reached.
stops.campa: He puts into English the life of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the Florentine who had posted nine hundred theses in Rome for all comers to dispute and was dead at thirty-one, and prints with it a set of Pico's letters and his rules of a Christian life. The subject is a nobleman who gave away his estates and refused every office offered him; the translator is a City lawyer with four small children, a practice, and twenty-five years of accepted office ahead of him. He dedicates the book to a nun of the Poor Clares.
suggested_refs: The Life of John Picus, Earl of Mirandula, printed in English by John Rastell
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas More' chronology

stops.name: Bucklersbury, City of London: the History of King Richard III
stops.date_confidence: Drafting begun c.1513 in parallel English and Latin versions, per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy chronology. Both versions were left unfinished and neither was published in More's lifetime; the date is the start of composition, not of any edition.
stops.campa: He begins a history of Richard III, working an English version and a Latin version side by side and finishing neither. What he writes is not a chronicle. It is a study of how a usurper talks: Buckingham working the crowd at the Guildhall, the sermon at Paul's Cross, the show of reluctance from a man accepting a crown he has already taken. A good deal of the matter comes out of Morton's household, where More carried dishes as a boy of twelve. He puts the manuscript down in the middle of a sentence and never picks it up.
suggested_refs: The History of King Richard III, English and Latin, unfinished, printed posthumously in the 1557 Workes
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas More' chronology

stops.name: Stadhuis, Bruges: the embassy that stalls
stops.date_confidence: Attested: royal commercial embassy to Flanders in 1515, Bruges and Antwerp (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; thomasmorestudies.org/chronology/). Month of arrival not fixed, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate tightened to Bruges City Hall on the Burg, approximately 51.2085, 3.2277; the dossier's 51.2094/3.2260 sat between the Burg and the Markt.
stops.campa: He crosses to Flanders on the king's business, one of a commission sent to argue out a quarrel over the wool trade with the envoys of Charles of Castile. The talks sit in the city hall on the Burg and then adjourn, because the other side has sent home for instructions and the instructions do not come. More has weeks with nothing in front of him in a foreign town. He starts writing an account of an island commonwealth with no money in it, no private property, no idleness and no lawyers, reported to him by a Portuguese sailor he is inventing as he goes.
suggested_refs: The Stadhuis on the Burg, Bruges, seat of the 1515 Anglo-Burgundian trade talks

stops.name: Stadhuis, Antwerp: Peter Giles and the frame of the fiction
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1515-1516 (Wikipedia, 'Utopia (book)'; thomasmorestudies.org). Split from the Bruges stop and dated 1516-01-01 to hold the travel order; the exact months of the Antwerp residence are not fixed by anything reached.
stops.campa: The embassy moves on to Antwerp, where he stays with Peter Giles, secretary of the city, a Greek scholar and a friend of Erasmus. Giles goes straight into the book as a character: it is he who brings the traveller Raphael Hythloday to a Thomas More sitting in a garden in Antwerp and sets the whole conversation going. The fiction is built so that every man named in it, except the one who has seen the island, is a real person with a real address that a reader could go and knock at. More sends the manuscript to Erasmus and asks him to find it a press.
suggested_refs: Pieter Gillis (Peter Giles), secretary of Antwerp, dedicatee and character of Utopia

stops.name: Louvain: the golden little book
stops.date_confidence: Attested: first Latin edition printed at Louvain, December 1516, by Dirk Martens under Erasmus's editorial supervision (Stanford Encyclopedia chronology; Wikipedia, 'Utopia (More book)'; Wikipedia, 'Dirk Martens'). CORRECTION CARRIED: the dossier credited the woodcuts to Ambrosius Holbein. Those belong to the 1518 Basel edition; the 1516 Louvain editio princeps carried a different, anonymous map. More himself was in London and did not attend the printing.
stops.campa: Dirk Martens prints the first edition here in December, under Erasmus's editorial hand. The author is three hundred miles away in London and never sees the press run. It is a small Latin book with a woodcut map of the island, an alphabet nobody speaks, and a title promising the best state of a commonwealth and a new island called Utopia, which in Greek is no place at all. Book Two describes the island. Book One argues whether a philosopher should take service with a king, cites Plato by name, and answers him.
suggested_refs: Libellus vere aureus... de optimo rei publicae statu deque nova insula Utopia, Louvain, Dirk Martens, December 1516
The 1518 Basel editions, with the Ambrosius Holbein map and frontispiece
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas More' chronology

stops.name: Cheapside, City of London: Evil May Day
stops.date_confidence: Attested: More was involved as a London officer in the suppression of the Evil May Day riot, 1 May 1517 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'), holding the under-sheriffship from 1510. The speech to the rioters, 'the Strangers' Case,' comes from the Elizabethan play Sir Thomas More, written roughly seventy years later; it is dramatic reconstruction and no contemporary record confirms he spoke it.
stops.campa: On May Day the apprentices of London rise against the foreign craftsmen living in the city, and the mob works through Cheapside and St Martin le Grand pulling down the strangers' houses. More, under-sheriff of London these seven years, goes out among them to talk them back and gets as far as the doors before the crowd turns on the argument. The Tower guns and the earls put the rising down; thirteen men are hanged. A play written seventy years later gives him a great speech to the rioters about what it is to be a stranger. Nobody who stood there wrote a word of it down.
suggested_refs: The Book of Sir Thomas More, Elizabethan play manuscript, and the 'Strangers' Case' speech attributed to Hand D

stops.name: Palace of Westminster: sworn of the king's council
stops.date_confidence: CONTESTED AND LEFT CONTESTED. The dossier asserted 1518 while sourcing it to Wikipedia, 'Thomas More', which in fact dates Master of Requests and the Privy Council membership to 1514. Luminarium and other chronologies give 1517 or 1518. The entry into full royal service is genuinely unfixed between 1514 and 1518; dated here at the late end of the range and flagged rather than resolved.
stops.campa: He goes into the king's service full time, as Master of Requests hearing the petitions of poor suitors and as a member of the council, travelling with the court wherever it moves. The year is not agreed: some accounts put both offices in 1514, others in 1517 or 1518, and none of them explains the others. Erasmus, who had pressed him toward it, writes afterward that More was dragged to that court rather than led to it. Henry keeps him at hand in the evenings for talk, for mathematics, and for the stars, sometimes past midnight.
suggested_refs: The office of Master of Requests and the Tudor Court of Requests

stops.name: Val d'Or, Balinghem: the Field of Cloth of Gold
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the kings met at the Val d'Or on Thursday 7 June 1520 and separated Sunday 24 June, and Wikipedia, 'Field of the Cloth of Gold' names More explicitly among the English guests. COORDINATE CORRECTED: the site is 50deg51'8.28"N 1deg55'22.44"E, that is 50.8523, 1.9229, in Balinghem between Guines and Ardres. The dossier's 50.8608/1.8654 was Guines town, about four kilometres off.
stops.campa: Henry VIII and Francis I meet on ground levelled for the purpose between Guines and Ardres: eighteen days of tents sewn with gold thread, tournaments, wrestling, and a temporary palace of timber and painted canvas with fountains of wine standing outside it. Four years earlier More had printed a book in which the islanders keep gold for chamber pots and for the fetters of slaves, so that their children learn early what to think of it. He is here anyway, as a councillor of the crown, named in the guest lists between Anne Boleyn's mother and her sister.
suggested_refs: The Val d'Or at Balinghem, site of the 7-24 June 1520 meeting
sources: Wikipedia, 'Field of the Cloth of Gold'

stops.name: Calais: knighted, and Under-Treasurer of the Exchequer
stops.date_confidence: Knighthood and the Under-Treasurership are attested for 1521 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; thomasmorestudies.org: '1521 Knighted'). The Calais diplomatic service in the same year is given by thomasmorestudies.org and is consistent with the Wolsey conference; month not fixed, defaulted. Coordinate tightened to approximately 50.9513, 1.8587; the dossier's figure sat about a kilometre north.
stops.campa: Knighted this year and made Under-Treasurer of the Exchequer, he crosses again for the long diplomatic sitting at Calais and Bruges in Cardinal Wolsey's train. Calais is the last English ground in France, a walled town with a garrison and the wool staple inside the wall, close enough that the council treats it as an office with a moat. He is forty-three: a knight, a salaried officer of the crown, the king's accounts under his hand, and a household back at Bucklersbury that has outgrown the street it stands in.
suggested_refs: The Calais Pale and the 1521 conference under Cardinal Wolsey

stops.name: Crosby Place, Bishopsgate: the Responsio ad Lutherum
stops.date_confidence: Publication of the Responsio ad Lutherum in 1523 under the pseudonym Gulielmus Rosseus is attested (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; Stanford Encyclopedia chronology). Month unknown, defaulted. CORRECTION CARRIED on the pin: Wikipedia, 'Crosby Hall, London' has More leasing the Bishopsgate property in 1519, purchasing in 1523, and in that same year selling on the remainder of the lease to Antonio Bonvisi. The dossier's 'leased 1523' inverted this. A property interest is not proof of continuous residence, and the pin is where his Bishopsgate interest lay, not a proven writing desk.
stops.campa: Henry VIII has published against Martin Luther and been given the title Defender of the Faith for it; Luther has answered the king in print and in kind. More writes the reply, in Latin, behind the borrowed name Gulielmus Rosseus, and matches Luther's coarseness page for page and then goes past it, in a performance his admirers have been explaining away ever since. He writes as a knight of the shire with a great house at Bishopsgate that was once Richard III's, and sells the remainder of that lease this same year to his friend the merchant Antonio Bonvisi.
suggested_refs: Responsio ad Lutherum, 1523, published as by Gulielmus Rosseus
Crosby Hall, Bishopsgate, later moved stone by stone to Chelsea
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas More' chronology

stops.name: Palace of Westminster: Speaker of the Commons
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Speaker of the House of Commons, 15 April to 13 August 1523 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'), with the petition to Henry VIII for freedom of speech in Parliament.
stops.campa: Chosen Speaker in April, he goes before Henry VIII with the customary petition and asks for something the custom does not contain: freedom of speech in the house, so that a member who speaks rashly or badly may be forgiven it, since men who are frightened of the king's displeasure cannot give the king true counsel. It is the earliest such request from a Speaker that survives. The Parliament grants the crown its subsidy in the end, and is dissolved on the thirteenth of August.
suggested_refs: The Speaker's petition of 1523, earliest surviving claim of parliamentary freedom of speech

stops.name: Chelsea: the new house on the river
stops.date_confidence: Genuinely disputed. thomasmorestudies.org/chronology/ gives 1524 for the move to Chelsea; Wikipedia, 'Thomas More' gives 1525. Rendered as c.1524-1525 and dated to the earlier reading. COORDINATE SEPARATED: the dossier used one point for both More's house and Chelsea Old Church. The church is 51.48306N, 0.17083W; the Beaufort House estate lay north-east of it and is pinned here at approximately 51.4847, -0.1712.
stops.campa: He builds west of the city, on the river at Chelsea, a house of some size with a great garden running down to the water, an orchard, a library, a gallery and a chapel of his own. Something over thirty people live in it: wife, children, sons and daughters in law, grandchildren, wards, the household fool Henry Patenson, and a menagerie. Henry VIII comes to dinner unannounced and walks in the garden an hour with his arm about More's neck. Roper, watching from the door, is impressed by it. His father in law is not.
stops.quote: I thank our Lord, son, I find His Grace my very good lord indeed, and I believe he doth as singularly favor me as any subject within this realm. Howbeit, son Roper, I may tell thee I have no cause to be proud thereof, for if my head could win him a castle in France (for then was there war between us) it should not fail to go.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.13
suggested_refs: The Beaufort House estate at Chelsea, More's riverside household from c.1524
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Palace of Westminster: Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: 31 December 1525 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'). Pinned at Westminster for the government office rather than at the Duchy's own Savoy premises, which are not fixed by any source reached.
stops.campa: On the last day of the year he is made Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, a court and an estate office running the crown's own northern lands with its own chancery and its own seal. It moves him out of the royal household and into the government proper, with the north of England and its revenues answering to him. He is forty-seven, with thirty people at Chelsea to keep. The City practice goes and the Under-Treasurership passes to another man; from here on he holds crown office and nothing else, and is paid for it by the crown alone.
suggested_refs: The Chancellorship of the Duchy of Lancaster and its separate chancery

stops.name: Chelsea: the school of the household
stops.date_confidence: Undated in the strict sense; the household regime at Chelsea is described by Roper and by Erasmus without a year attached. Dated 1526 purely to order the segment between the move and Holbein's visit. The quote is Roper's, given without a date in his text.
stops.campa: The Chelsea house runs as a school. His daughters, their husbands and the wards read Greek and Latin, mathematics, astronomy and the Fathers on one timetable; Margaret's Latin letters go round among scholars who at first refuse to believe a woman wrote them. There is a lesson before supper and prayers after it, and no cards. Erasmus calls the place a school and academy of the Christian religion. More tells the children, who are being carried along by good example on every side of them, that they are having it easy.
stops.quote: It is now no mastery for you children to go to heaven, for everybody giveth you good counsel, everybody giveth you good example, you see virtue rewarded and vice punished, so that you are carried up to heaven even by the chins.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.16
suggested_refs: Margaret Roper's Latin correspondence, circulated among the northern humanists
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text
Erasmus to Ulrich von Hutten, 23 July 1519

stops.name: Chelsea: Holbein in the house
stops.date_confidence: The individual portrait is dated 1527 by standard art history and by Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; the panel is in the Frick Collection, New York, whose own provenance page could not be fetched (404) and is therefore carried on the Wikipedia cross-reference. The lost group portrait is dated c.1527. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Hans Holbein the Younger arrives in England with a letter from Erasmus and lodges at Chelsea, and in the course of the stay paints the master of the house in a fur-collared gown with the chain of office lying across his shoulders and a face doing three things at once. He also paints the whole household together, eleven figures with their books and their ages lettered beside them, the first group portrait of its kind north of the Alps. The single panel survives and hangs in New York. The group picture burned in the eighteenth century and is known from a copy.
suggested_refs: Holbein's Sir Thomas More, 1527, Frick Collection, New York
Rowland Lockey's 1592 copy of the lost Holbein household group, Nostell Priory, Yorkshire (53.6527, -1.3900), commissioned by the More family and held the most faithful to the destroyed original

stops.name: Chelsea Old Church: the private chapel
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the south chapel was rebuilt in 1528 as Sir Thomas More's private chapel, with the date carved on a chancel pillar capital (Wikipedia, 'Chelsea Old Church'). COORDINATE CORRECTED to 51.48306N, 0.17083W and separated from the pin for More's own house, which the dossier had collapsed into the same point.
stops.campa: A few hundred yards downriver from the house he rebuilds the south chapel of the parish church as his own. It is a small thing, a single bay off the south side of the chancel, and the only part of the building he touches. The year is cut into the capitals of the chancel pillars, where it can still be read. This is where the household hears mass, the whole thirty of them walking down from the house together and back again. He is Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster while the masons are at work; within a year the great seal of England will be in his hands.
suggested_refs: The More Chapel, Chelsea Old Church, rebuilt 1528, date carved on the chancel capitals

stops.name: Cambrai, prince-bishopric in the Habsburg Netherlands: the peace
stops.date_confidence: The treaty was signed 5 August 1529 and Cambrai in that year was NOT French: Wikipedia, 'Treaty of Cambrai' calls it the centre of a principality-bishopric in the Netherlands, now the French department of Nord. The dossier's label 'Cambrai, France' is anachronistic and is corrected here. More's own participation could NOT be independently confirmed: the Treaty of Cambrai article names no English envoys, and the Cuthbert Tunstall article credits Tunstall alone. The claim rests on thomasmorestudies.org and is tagged [R].
stops.campa: He is sent to Cambrai, a prince-bishopric of the Habsburg Netherlands and not yet French ground, where Margaret of Austria and Louise of Savoy are sitting down to settle the war between a nephew and a son. The treaty is signed on the fifth of August, England is a party to it, and the peace it makes holds for seven years. That More was in the delegation is recorded by the Center for Thomas More Studies chronology and by nothing else that could be reached. The treaty's own record names no English envoys at all. Whether he stood in that room is not a thing the sources will say.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Cambrai, 5 August 1529, the Paix des Dames
sources: Wikipedia, 'Cuthbert Tunstall' (checked, does not name More)

stops.name: Palace of Westminster: the great seal after Wolsey
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: Lord Chancellor of England from 26 October 1529 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'). The Dialogue Concerning Heresies is attested to 1529 without a month and is carried into this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: Wolsey falls for failing to get the king his annulment, and on the twenty-sixth of October the great seal goes into the hands of a layman, the first chancellor in living memory who is not a bishop. More takes the oath as Lord Chancellor of England. He works the Chancery backlog down, sits in Star Chamber, and in the same year publishes the Dialogue Concerning Heresies, arguing in plain English against the English books coming in from Antwerp. He holds the seal for two years and seven months.
suggested_refs: A Dialogue Concerning Heresies, 1529
The Court of Chancery and Star Chamber under More's chancellorship

stops.name: Chelsea: the walk along the water
stops.date_confidence: Undated in Roper, who places it at Chelsea without a year; the internal reference to the king's matter puts it in the chancellorship or just before. Dated 1530 purely to order the segment. Roper wrote the scene about thirty years after the fact, from memory, in Mary's reign.
stops.campa: Roper walks with him in the garden at Chelsea, down along the water, and the Lord Chancellor of England says that he would agree to be tied into a sack and thrown into this river, here, at once, if three things could be settled in Christendom: peace among the Christian princes, one faith in the church, and a good end to the king's matter. Roper sets it down thirty years afterward, from memory, in a house where the speaker has become a martyr and the king he served is dead.
stops.quote: Now would to our Lord, son Roper, upon condition that three things were well established in Christendom, I were put into a sack, and here presently cast into the Thames.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.14
suggested_refs: The Chelsea river frontage below More's garden
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Palace of Westminster: the seal given back
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: resignation as Lord Chancellor, 16 May 1532, citing ill health (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'). That the true reason was the break with Rome is the universal reading and is not itself a documented statement by More, who gave no reason but his health.
stops.campa: The clergy of England submit to Henry as supreme head so far as the law of Christ allows. The next day More gives back the great seal. The reason entered is his health, and his health is genuinely bad; the reason everybody reads is the other one. From this day he says nothing about the king's marriage that anyone will afterwards be able to prove he said. He is fifty-four, out of office, without a salary, with a household of thirty at Chelsea and a chest complaint.
suggested_refs: The Submission of the Clergy, 15 May 1532

stops.name: Chelsea: the coronation not attended
stops.date_confidence: Attested: More refused to attend Anne Boleyn's coronation, 1 June 1533 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; Luminarium). The detail of the twenty pounds sent by three bishops for a gown is Roper's and is [R]. The questioning over Elizabeth Barton, the Holy Maid of Kent, by Cromwell's agents is attested for 1534 and is carried into this stop.
stops.campa: Anne Boleyn is crowned at Westminster on the first of June, and three bishops send More twenty pounds to buy himself a gown for it. He keeps the money and stays at Chelsea. No statute requires a private gentleman out of office to watch a coronation, so there is nothing there to prosecute; but an absence is a legible thing at a small court, and it is read. Within the year Thomas Cromwell's men have him in a room, asking about Elizabeth Barton, the Holy Maid of Kent, whether he encouraged her prophecies against the marriage, and what exactly he put in the letter he wrote to her.
stops.quote: We may not look at our pleasure to go to heaven in featherbeds; it is not the way, for our Lord himself went thither with great pain and by many tribulations, which was the path wherein he walked thither, for the servant may not look to be in better case than his master.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.16, said to the household in sickness or trouble; Roper gives no date
suggested_refs: The attainder of Elizabeth Barton, the Holy Maid of Kent, 1534
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Lambeth Palace: the oath refused
stops.date_confidence: Attested: summoned before the commissioners at Lambeth 13 April 1534, committed to the Tower 17 April (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; thomasmorestudies.org gives the imprisonment as 17 April). Same coordinate correction as the earlier Lambeth stop: 51.49556, -0.11972, not the dossier's -0.1219.
stops.campa: Summoned back across the river to Lambeth on the thirteenth of April, he is shown the oath appended to the Act of Succession and told to swear it. He answers that he will swear to the succession itself, since Parliament may lawfully settle who inherits the crown, but not to the preamble, which puts the king over the church and repudiates Rome. Asked why not, he will not say. A man who gives his reasons can be argued with and quoted; a man who is silent has done nothing the statute names. Four days later they take him downriver.
suggested_refs: The Act of Succession 1534 and the oath appended to it
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Tower of London: fifteen months
stops.date_confidence: Attested: imprisoned in the Tower from 17 April 1534 to 6 July 1535, writing A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation and the unfinished De tristitia Christi there (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; Roper). The specific cell, the Bell Tower, is the standard tradition rather than a documented assignment and is [R].
stops.campa: He is lodged in the Bell Tower and stays fifteen months. Margaret visits, is sent in to persuade him, fails at it, and keeps coming. He writes A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation, set among Hungarians waiting for the Turk to arrive at the gate, and begins De tristitia Christi on the agony in the garden, and stops in the middle of a word. John Fisher is held in the same fortress on the same refusal. The books go first, carried out by Richard Rich and a party of men. Then the paper and the ink go. The last letters are written with a piece of coal.
suggested_refs: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation, written in the Tower, printed 1553
De tristitia Christi, unfinished, the autograph now at Valencia
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas More' chronology

stops.name: Westminster Hall: the trial
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1 July 1535 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; the Paris newsletter of 4 August 1535). CONTRADICTION FLAGGED, NOT RESOLVED: famous-trials.com's report of the trial carries a conflicting May date. The 1 July date is followed here because two independent sources give it, but the discrepancy stands unexplained. Conviction in about a quarter of an hour is attested.
stops.campa: He is brought up the river to Westminster Hall on the first of July, before a special commission that includes Anne Boleyn's father, her brother and her uncle. The case rests on one man, Richard Rich, solicitor general, who swears that More denied the king's supremacy to him in the Tower while the books were being carried out. Two other men were in the room, and both say they heard nothing. More answers Rich on his oath, is convicted in about a quarter of an hour, and then, for the first time in fifteen months, says out loud what he thinks.
stops.quote: In good faith, Master Rich, I am sorrier for your perjury than for my own peril.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.50
suggested_refs: Westminster Hall, seat of the special commission of 1 July 1535
The Paris Newsletter account of More's trial and execution, 4 August 1535, in Letters and Papers, Foreign and Domestic, Henry VIII, vol. 8, no. 996
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Westminster Hall: the indictment answered after judgment
stops.date_confidence: Same session, 1 July 1535, after the verdict. Roper reports that More interrupted Lord Chancellor Audley before sentence to claim the prisoner's old right to be asked why judgment should not be given. The speeches are Roper's text and the Paris Newsletter's, and the two accounts differ in wording though not in substance; both are given in the sources. Split from the preceding stop so that the argument, which is the only public statement of his position he ever made, is not buried inside the account of Rich.
stops.campa: Convicted, he stops the Lord Chancellor before sentence can be passed and claims the prisoner's ancient right to be asked why judgment should not be given against him. Then, after fifteen months of saying nothing, he says it: that the indictment stands on an act of Parliament directly repugnant to the laws of God and His Holy Church, whose government no temporal prince may take upon himself. The Paris newsletter has him answer the bench that for one bishop of their opinion he has a hundred saints of his, and for one parliament all the general councils of a thousand years.
stops.quote: More have I not to say, my lords, but that like as the blessed apostle St. Paul... was present, and consented to the death of St. Stephen, and kept their clothes that stoned him to death, and yet be they now both twain holy saints in heaven, and shall continue there friends for ever, so I verily trust, and shall therefore right heartily pray, that though your lordships have now here in earth been judges to my condemnation, we may yet hereafter in heaven merrily all meet together, to our everlasting salvation.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.54
suggested_refs: The Paris Newsletter, 4 August 1535, an independent report of the same speeches in different words
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text
Letters and Papers, Foreign and Domestic, Henry VIII, vol. 8, no. 996 (ed. Brewer & Gairdner, 1882)

stops.name: Old Swan Stairs and the Tower wharf: parting from Kingston
stops.date_confidence: Roper's scene, undated within the day but placed immediately after the trial, 1 July 1535. Pinned at the Tower landing rather than at Old Swan Stairs upriver, since the parting from Kingston and Margaret's interception both happen at the Tower end of the passage.
stops.campa: The barge brings him back downriver to the Tower landing, and Sir William Kingston, constable of the Tower, who has walked a good many men up from that water, cannot keep from weeping as he walks this one. More does the comforting. Roper, watching from the crowd on the wharf, writes that he had never seen the constable so unmanned in his life. Margaret is waiting there. She breaks through the guard and the halberds, takes hold of her father in front of everybody, is pulled off him, and comes back and does it again.
stops.quote: Good Master Kingston, trouble not yourself, but be of good cheer; for I will pray for you, and my good lady your wife, that we may meet in heaven together, where we shall be merry for ever and ever.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.55
suggested_refs: The Tower wharf and the water gate, landing place after the Westminster trial
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Tower of London: the last letter to Margaret
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the last letter to Margaret Roper, written with a coal on 5 July 1535, the day before the execution (Roper). St Thomas's Eve and the octave of St Peter both fall on 6 July, which is why he asks for that day.
stops.campa: On the evening of the fifth he writes to Margaret with a piece of coal, having no ink left. He sends her his hair shirt, which he does not want found on the body, and the scourge with it, and tells her not to be sorry about the timing, since tomorrow is the eve of St Thomas and the octave of St Peter and he would rather go then than later. He blesses the children by name, and the grandchildren, and the godchildren, and Alice, and the maids. Then he writes a line about the way she kissed him on the wharf.
stops.quote: I cumber you, good Margaret, much, but I would be sorry if it should be any longer than tomorrow, for tomorrow is St. Thomas's Even, and the Utas of St. Peter. And therefore tomorrow long I to go to God... I never liked your manner towards me better than when you kissed me last. For I like when daughterly love and dear charity have no leisure to look to worldly courtesy.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.56
suggested_refs: More's Tower correspondence, written in coal after the writing materials were removed
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Tower Hill: the scaffold
stops.date_confidence: Attested: beheaded on Tower Hill, 6 July 1535, aged 57, the sentence for treason commuted to beheading. THE FAMOUS LINE IS TAGGED [R] AND IS NOT PRINTED AS A QUOTE HERE. It appears in no primary source that could be reached: 'good servant', 'king's good servant' and 'God's first' are all absent from Roper's Life entirely, and the Paris Newsletter of 4 August 1535 gives only reported speech, 'protesting that he died his faithful servant, and God's first' (the CTMS transcription reads 'and', the 1882 Letters and Papers translation 'but'). Note the further drift from 'faithful servant' to 'good servant' in the popular version. The executioner quote below is Roper's and is direct.
stops.campa: He is brought out to the scaffold on Tower Hill on the morning of the sixth, the sentence of hanging and quartering commuted by the king to beheading. He asks the crowd to pray for him, and to pray that the king be given good counsel. The only contemporary account, a newsletter written in Paris a month afterward, reports the rest in the third person: that he protested he died the king's faithful servant, and God's first. The famous line in the first person is nobody's transcript of anything. Then he turns and speaks to the man with the axe.
stops.quote: Pluck up thy spirits, man, and be not afraid to do thine office; my neck is very short; take heed therefore thou strike not awry, for saving of thine honesty.
stops.quote_source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c.1556), ed. Wegemer & Smith, Center for Thomas More Studies, p.58
suggested_refs: The scaffold site on Tower Hill
The Paris Newsletter, 4 August 1535, the only contemporary account of the execution
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text
Letters and Papers, Foreign and Domestic, Henry VIII, vol. 8, no. 996

segments.name: The Body, the Head, and the Altar

stops.name: Chapel Royal of St Peter ad Vincula, Tower of London: the body
stops.date_confidence: Attested: buried in St Peter ad Vincula inside the Tower, in an unmarked grave, the same day (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'). Coordinate tightened to approximately 51.5085, -0.0770 at the Tower's north-west corner; the dossier's -0.0762 sat nearer the White Tower. The competing tradition that the body lies at Chelsea Old Church is unsubstantiated and is flagged rather than resolved.
stops.campa: The body is carried the short way down from the hill into the Tower precinct the same day and put into the ground in the Chapel Royal of St Peter ad Vincula. The grave is not marked, and no record says which part of the floor it lies under. This is the ordinary burying place for those executed inside the Tower and on the hill above it, and by the summer of 1535 there is already a fair number of them beneath that pavement. Chelsea Old Church has claimed the body since. The claim is local tradition and rests on nothing.
suggested_refs: The Chapel Royal of St Peter ad Vincula, Tower of London
sources: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Fordham Sourcebooks text

stops.name: Old London Bridge, the drawbridge gate: the head
stops.date_confidence: The head was parboiled and displayed on London Bridge, attested. CORRECTION CARRIED: the dossier put it on the southern gatehouse, which is anachronistic by four decades. Wikipedia, 'Old London Bridge' has traitors' heads exhibited on the DRAWBRIDGE TOWER mid-span, the Southwark stone gate taking over that function only after the drawbridge tower was replaced in 1577-1579. Coordinate moved to approximately 51.5065, -0.0873 on the old bridge line, which stood about thirty metres east of the present bridge. Margaret's recovery of the head is [R]: famous-trials.com confirms only that it stood 'for some Months' and that she 'bought it'; the bribed bridge-keeper and the rescue from the river are later elaboration.
stops.campa: The head is parboiled and set on a pole above the bridge, on the drawbridge gate in the middle of the span, where the heads of traitors are shown to everyone crossing. The stone gatehouse at the Southwark end takes over that duty only after the drawbridge tower is rebuilt in the 1570s. By the Paris newsletter's reckoning it stands there some months. Then it is gone. The family says Margaret bought it before it could be tipped into the river, and the family has always been the only source there is for what happened next.
suggested_refs: The drawbridge tower of Old London Bridge, replaced 1577-1579

stops.name: St Dunstan's Church, Canterbury: the Roper vault
stops.date_confidence: Tradition throughout, tagged [R]. Margaret Roper died in 1544; the chain of custody from London Bridge to the Roper vault at St Dunstan's is family and ecclesiastical tradition, not continuous documentation. COORDINATE CORRECTED to 51.2836583N, 1.0708139E per Wikipedia, 'St Dunstan's, Canterbury'; the dossier gave two different wrong latitudes in two different lenses. DATE CORRECTED: the dossier's '1997 vault opening' appears to be a corruption of 1978, the opening reported in H. O. Albin, 'Opening of the Roper Vault in St. Dunstan's Canterbury', Moreana (1979). The 2025 exhumation proposal and the GBP 50,000 figure in the dossier could not be confirmed anywhere and are not printed. Margaret's own burial place is contradicted between Canterbury and Chelsea Old Church, and the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: Margaret Roper dies in 1544, having kept the head in spices for nine years, and the head goes into the Roper family vault beneath the chapel at St Dunstan's outside the walls of Canterbury, the church of her husband's people. A niche in the wall of the vault is said to hold it still. The vault has been opened and examined once, and the account of that opening, published in Moreana, describes fragmentary remains rather than an intact skull. Whether Margaret herself lies here or at Chelsea, the sources flatly disagree, and neither of them gives way.
suggested_refs: H. O. Albin, 'Opening of the Roper Vault in St. Dunstan's Canterbury and Thoughts on the Burial of William and Margaret Roper', Moreana (1979)

stops.name: Vatican City: beatified, then canonized with Fisher
stops.date_confidence: Both dates attested and both were missing their day in the dossier. Leo XIII's beatification decree is dated 29 December 1886, the same decree under which Wikipedia, 'Forty Martyrs of England and Wales' records eleven beatifications on that day. Pius XI canonized More jointly with John Fisher on 19 May 1935 (Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'). The stop is dated to the canonization and carries the beatification in the campa.
stops.campa: Leo XIII beatifies him on the twenty-ninth of December 1886, in a decree covering a group of the English martyrs together. Forty-nine years after that, on the nineteenth of May 1935, Pius XI canonizes him jointly with John Fisher, the bishop who refused the same oath and went to the same block a fortnight before him. Four hundred years have passed since the beheading. In that same year an English professor of literature, R. W. Chambers, publishes the biography that turns him back into a historical subject rather than a devotional one.
suggested_refs: R. W. Chambers, Thomas More (1935)
Wikipedia, 'Forty Martyrs of England and Wales', on the decree of 29 December 1886

stops.name: Chelsea Old Church: the chapel that survived the mine
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the church was hit by a parachute mine on 14 April 1941; the More Chapel sustained the least damage of the standing fabric. More's chapel reopened in 1950, the chancel and Lawrence Chapel in May 1954, and the whole church was reconsecrated in May 1958 (Wikipedia, 'Chelsea Old Church'). The Leslie Cubitt Bevis statue outside, facing the river, is attested by the same source without a date.
stops.campa: On the night of the fourteenth of April a parachute mine falls on Chelsea Old Church and brings down the tower, the nave and most of the roof. The south chapel he rebuilt in 1528 takes the least damage of anything left standing, and the capitals with the date on them come through it. His chapel reopens in 1950, the chancel and the Lawrence Chapel in 1954, and the whole church is reconsecrated in 1958. A statue of him by Leslie Cubitt Bevis sits outside now, on the churchyard side, facing the river he used to be rowed down to work.
suggested_refs: The More Chapel, Chelsea Old Church, and the Leslie Cubitt Bevis statue facing the Thames

stops.name: Vatican City: patron of statesmen and politicians
stops.date_confidence: Attested and verified directly against vatican.va: the apostolic letter is dated 31 October 2000 and reads 'I establish and declare Saint Thomas More the heavenly Patron of Statesmen and Politicians.' TITLE CORRECTED: the incipit is 'E sancti Thomae Mori', not the dossier's 'Ex Sancti Thomae Mori'.
stops.campa: On the last day of October in the Jubilee year, John Paul II signs an apostolic letter, E sancti Thomae Mori, declaring Thomas More the heavenly patron of statesmen and politicians. The letter is about the fifteen months in the Bell Tower and the quarter of an hour in Westminster Hall; its argument is that he served the state as far as conscience let him and no further, and that the place where he stopped is the place the office most needs marked. Utopia is not mentioned. The operative sentence reads: I establish and declare Saint Thomas More the heavenly Patron of Statesmen and Politicians.
suggested_refs: John Paul II, motu proprio E sancti Thomae Mori, 31 October 2000, vatican.va
